question: What is the main purpose of taking a nutrition history in nursing practice?

options.A: To gather information about a patient's food intake and eating habits
options.B: To strictly calculate the exact daily financial cost of groceries
options.C: To diagnose rare genetic metabolic disorders immediately
options.D: To prescribe specific medical diets without consulting a doctor

explanation: A nutrition history focuses directly on understanding what and how a patient eats to guide their care. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h1)

question: Why is a nutrition history considered a vital part of a standard patient admission assessment?

options.A: It helps catch early warning signs of poor nourishment before severe illness develops
options.B: It replaces the need to check vital signs or physical examination findings
options.C: It ensures the hospital kitchen meets local food safety inspection standards
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will never experience any weight loss

explanation: Early identification of dietary issues allows nurses to intervene before nutritional problems turn into major health complications. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h1)

question: What is the primary goal of a dietary assessment?

options.A: To determine the exact brand of food the patient prefers to buy
options.B: To evaluate nutritional status and check for adequate nutrient intake
options.C: To calculate the patient's daily physical exercise routine accurately
options.D: To test for food allergies using a series of skin prick procedures

explanation: Evaluating whether a patient gets enough essential nutrients is the central objective of any dietary assessment. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h2)

question: A nurse uses a dietary assessment to establish a baseline. What does this mean for patient care?

options.A: It provides a starting point to measure future nutritional changes and treatment progress
options.B: It acts as a permanent record that cannot be altered during the hospital stay
options.C: It proves that the patient has no underlying metabolic diseases
options.D: It serves as the final clearance for the patient to be discharged home

explanation: Establishing a baseline gives healthcare providers a reference point to see if interventions are helping or if the patient's condition is worsening. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h2)

question: Which of the following is included in a comprehensive nutrition history?

options.C: Recent travel history outside the country

explanation: Medical conditions and medications heavily influence how the body absorbs and uses nutrients, making them essential parts of a nutrition history. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h3)

question: A patient takes a daily diuretic medication that causes frequent urination. Why must a nurse note this during a nutrition history?

options.A: Medications have no bearing on nutritional status and can be ignored
options.B: Patients on diuretics are legally prohibited from eating high-protein foods
options.C: Diuretics completely replace the need for dietary fiber in older adults
options.D: Certain medications can affect nutrient levels and fluid balance in the body

explanation: Many drugs interact with nutrients, alter appetite, or cause losses of vitamins and minerals, which a nurse must account for. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h3)

question: What is the main limitation of using a 24-hour dietary recall?

options.A: It relies heavily on the patient's memory and may not show normal eating habits
options.B: It is too expensive for routine use in busy outpatient clinics
options.C: It requires the patient to write down every meal for an entire month
options.D: It only measures fluid intake and ignores solid foods entirely

explanation: A single day may represent an unusual eating day, such as a holiday or a day of illness, and patients often forget items they consumed. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h4)

question: When is a food diary or food record most effective for collecting nutrition data?

options.A: When the nurse wants to avoid interacting directly with the patient
options.B: When immediate emergency surgery is required within the next hour
options.C: When the patient is motivated and capable of recording meals as they happen
options.D: When the patient has severe memory loss or advanced dementia

explanation: Food diaries require active participation and clear recording in real-time to provide accurate data. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h4)

question: What does the term 'food security' refer to in nutritional nursing assessments?

options.A: Having reliable access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food
options.B: Eating only foods that have been certified organic by government agencies
options.C: Keeping hospital kitchen supplies locked away from pests
options.D: Storing perishable groceries at the correct refrigerator temperature

explanation: Food security means an individual has physical and economic access to the food they need for an active, healthy life. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h5)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to understand a patient's cultural or religious food practices?

options.A: It guarantees that the patient will never develop chronic illnesses
options.B: It helps create realistic and acceptable dietary plans the patient will actually follow
options.C: It allows the nurse to change the patient's cultural beliefs to match hospital standards
options.D: It is only required for legal documentation and has no clinical value

explanation: Dietary recommendations that clash with a patient's cultural or religious values are rarely sustained at home. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h5)

question: Which physical sign is most commonly associated with iron deficiency anemia?

options.A: Swollen and bleeding joints in the hands
options.B: Rapid and excessive growth of fingernails
options.C: Yellow discoloration of the whites of the eyes
options.D: Pale conjunctiva inside the lower eyelids

explanation: Low red blood cell counts or hemoglobin levels often manifest as pallor, which is easily seen in the inner lining of the eyelids. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h6)

question: What does noticeable muscle wasting in the temples and shoulders suggest about a patient?

options.B: Normal aging with no clinical significance
options.D: Temporary dehydration from lack of water

explanation: When the body lacks sufficient protein and calories over time, it breaks down muscle mass for energy, leading to visible wasting in areas like the temples and shoulders. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h6)

question: Which of the following is an example of objective nutritional documentation?

options.A: Patient hates hospital food because it tastes bland and boring
options.B: Patient reports eating fresh vegetables once a week and skipping breakfast
options.C: Patient is lazy and refuses to eat the nutritious food provided by the hospital
options.D: Patient has a terrible diet and clearly does not care about health

explanation: Objective documentation relies on factual, descriptive statements without personal opinions or judgmental language. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h7)

question: Why is accurate nutritional documentation important among members of the healthcare team?

options.A: It replaces the need for verbal shift handovers entirely
options.B: It prevents the hospital from having to buy specialized nutritional supplements
options.C: It ensures clear communication between nurses, doctors, and dietitians for coordinated care
options.D: It is only used for insurance billing and has no role in clinical treatment

explanation: Clear notes allow every healthcare provider involved in the patient's care to understand their nutritional status and treatment plan. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h7)

question: What tool can nurses use to help patients estimate portion sizes more accurately?

options.A: A standard household measuring cup for liquid medications only
options.B: A complex laboratory blood test for vitamin levels
options.C: Visual aids like food models or picture charts
options.D: Strict financial receipts from local grocery stores

explanation: Patients often struggle to describe portion sizes in grams or cups, so visual aids make it easier for them to show how much they ate. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h8)

question: Which practice is NOT recommended when conducting a nutrition history with a patient?

options.A: Asking open-ended questions about daily meal routines
options.B: Creating a comfortable and open environment to build trust
options.C: Re-evaluating the patient's nutrition status as their condition changes
options.D: Using judgmental language when the patient reports poor eating habits

explanation: Judgmental language makes patients defensive and less honest about their true habits, which hinders proper care. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h8)
